teile.einleitung: The pan flute is an ancient wind instrument made of many pipes fixed side by side. Each pipe gives its own note, and the longest sounds the lowest. The pan flute is a wonderful example for understanding how vibrating air turns into music.
wichtigste: A pan flute consists of many pipes of different lengths side by side.
The pipes are closed at the bottom and open at the top.
You play it by blowing across the top edge of a pipe.
Each pipe normally gives only one note.
The longer the pipe, the lower the note.
The instrument is named after the Greek shepherd god Pan.
Pan flutes used to be made mostly of reed or bamboo, and they are still very popular in the Andes of South America today.

abschnitte.text: A pan flute consists of several **pipes** arranged by length like a staircase. They are held together with string, raffia or a crosspiece of wood. The pipes are closed at the bottom, for example by a natural knot in the bamboo or a plug. In the past, reed or bamboo was mostly used; today there are also pan flutes made of wood, plastic or metal.

You hold the pipe against your lower lip and blow a fine stream of air across the **edge**. The stream of air is split at the edge and sets the air inside the pipe vibrating. This **air column** vibrates at a certain frequency, which we hear as a note. It sounds similar when you blow across the neck of an empty bottle.

The pitch depends on the length of the air column. In a long pipe, the sound wave takes longer to travel there and back, the **frequency** is lower and the note is deeper. Short pipes sound high accordingly. Because the pipes are closed at the bottom, a pipe sounds about an octave lower than a pipe of the same length that is open at both ends. By changing the angle of blowing, a skilled player can bend a note up or down a little.

The name comes from **Greek mythology**. Pan was a god of shepherds and flocks, half man and half goat. According to the legend, the nymph Syrinx turned into reeds while fleeing from him, and Pan then cut his flute from them. That is why the pan flute is also called syrinx in Greek.

Pan flutes existed thousands of years ago in many parts of the world, for example in China, Europe and South America. In the **Andes**, for example in Peru and Bolivia, it is called siku or zampoña and is part of traditional music. In Romania, a curved pan flute called the nai is played. In Switzerland, too, you often hear pan flutes from street musicians and in music schools.

begriffe.erklaerung: The air inside a pipe that vibrates when you blow.
How often something vibrates per second; it decides the pitch.
The distance between two notes in which the higher one vibrates twice as fast.
A nature spirit in the form of a young woman from the Greek legends.

gewusst: You can make a simple pan flute from drinking straws closed at the bottom with modelling clay.
In biology, the voice organ of birds is also called the syrinx, like the pan flute.
A pipe that is half as long sounds about an octave higher.

teile.einleitung: A paper aeroplane is a small aircraft folded from a single sheet of paper. It has no engine but glides through the air after being thrown. By making and trying them out, you learn in a playful way how flying works.
wichtigste: A paper aeroplane is folded from a sheet of paper, without scissors or glue.
As it glides, the air under the wings carries it.
Smooth, symmetrical wings are important; crumpled paper flies badly.
If the nose is too heavy, the plane dives steeply.
Small flaps bent upwards at the back of the wings help it stay up longer.
It is best to throw it gently forwards.
The folding of figures out of paper is called origami.

abschnitte.text: A paper aeroplane is a **glider**, an aircraft without any drive. It gets its energy only from the throw. After that it sinks slowly and glides forwards as it does, much like a glider aircraft. Well-known models are the pointed dart, which flies fast and far, and wider gliders that float in the air for a long time.

Four things act on it in flight: gravity pulls it down, **lift** keeps it up, the throw gives it momentum forwards and **air resistance** slows it down. The wings are tilted slightly and push the oncoming air downwards. As a result, the air pushes the plane upwards. For it to fly smoothly, the centre of gravity and the shape of the wings must match well.

The point where the weight of the plane is concentrated is called the **centre of gravity**. If it is slightly in front of the middle, the plane flies steadily straight ahead, which is why the nose is usually folded several times. But if the nose is far too heavy, it tips forwards and dives steeply. If it is too light, it climbs, slows down and then stalls.

Fold neatly and press every crease sharp with your fingernail. Both wings must be exactly the same, or the plane will turn off to the side. If you bend small **flaps** slightly upwards at the back of the wings, the nose lifts and it glides for longer. Throw it gently and straight forwards, not steeply upwards. Indoors it flies straighter than outdoors, because there is no wind to disturb it.

Paper was invented in China, and folding has a long tradition in East Asia. The art of folding figures out of paper is called **origami** in Japanese. By the classic rules, a paper aeroplane needs no scissors, glue or sticky tape. Today there are competitions for the furthest and longest flights, and paper aeroplane competitions are held in many Swiss schools too.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of the air that pushes a wing upwards.
The point at which you could balance an object.
An aircraft without an engine that flies forwards while slowly sinking.
The Japanese art of folding figures out of paper.

gewusst: The world record for the furthest paper aeroplane throw is over 70 metres, which is more than the width of a football pitch.
With a small paper clip on the nose, you can easily shift the centre of gravity of a paper aeroplane.
Large aircraft also have movable flaps at the back of their wings, much like a trimmed paper aeroplane.

teile.einleitung: In a parallel circuit, several electrical devices are connected side by side to the same power source. Each device has its own branch through which current flows. This is also how all the lamps and sockets in a home are connected.
wichtigste: In a parallel circuit, each device has its own branch on the same source.
If one lamp fails, the others stay lit.
Each branch has the same voltage as the source.
Two identical lamps in parallel on a battery shine as brightly as a single lamp.
The total current is the sum of the currents in the branches.
If you connect another device in parallel, the total current increases.
The point where the circuit splits is called a junction.

abschnitte.text: In a parallel circuit, the circuit splits into several **branches** that lie side by side. Each branch contains a device, for example a lamp. The place where the wire branches is called a **junction**. The opposite is the series circuit, in which all the devices hang one after the other in a single loop.

Each branch has the full **voltage** of the source across it. That is why two identical lamps connected in parallel to a battery shine as brightly as a single lamp on the same battery. If one lamp burns out, only its branch is broken. The other lamp still gets current and stays lit.

The current from the source splits up between the branches at the junction. If 0.2 amperes flow through one lamp and 0.3 amperes through the other, 0.5 amperes flow in the main wire. You can also calculate the other way round: if 1.2 amperes flow in the main wire and 0.5 amperes in one branch, there are 0.7 amperes in the other. This rule is called the **junction rule** and was described by Gustav Robert Kirchhoff in 1845.

In Switzerland, all the sockets and lamps in a home are connected in parallel to the 230-volt mains. That way, every device gets the right voltage, and each one can be switched on and off separately. But every extra device increases the **total current** in the supply wire. If it gets too large, the **fuse** switches off so that the wires do not overheat.

Batteries can also be connected in parallel: the voltage stays the same, but together they last longer. For **resistance**, something surprising applies in a parallel circuit. The more branches there are, the smaller the total resistance becomes, because the current has more paths. Two identical resistors in parallel together give only half the resistance.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of the circuit that lies next to other parts.
A point where one wire splits into several wires.
What drives the current, measured in volts.
How much electricity flows, measured in amperes.
A circuit in which all the devices lie one after the other in a loop.

gewusst: Many modern fairy lights are wired in parallel so that the whole string does not go out when one bulb breaks.
If you plug too many powerful devices into a multi-socket adaptor, the wire can get dangerously hot.
The junction rule holds because no current is lost or added along the way.

teile.einleitung: A pedal is the part of a bike that you push with your feet to make it go. A normal bicycle has two pedals, which are attached to the cranks and turn in a circle. The force of our legs is cleverly turned into a turning movement.
wichtigste: A normal bicycle has two pedals.
The pedals sit on the cranks and turn in a circle as you ride.
It is best to push the pedal with the ball of your foot.
In Switzerland, pedals must have orange or yellow reflectors.
Uphill, riders sometimes stand up to push with their whole body weight.
With clipless pedals, the shoe clicks into the pedal.
The crank works like a lever.

abschnitte.text: The pedal is the surface you push with to drive a bike. It is attached so that it can turn on the **crank**, an arm connected to the bottom bracket axle. The two cranks are exactly opposite each other, so one foot is always up and one down. The turning movement is passed to the back wheel through the chainring and the **chain**.

The crank is a **lever**: the longer the crank, the less force you need to turn it. The turning effect of a force is called **torque**. It is greatest when the crank is horizontal and you push straight down. Uphill, cyclists often stand up so that they can push on the pedal with their whole body weight.

It is best to push the pedal with the **ball of your foot** and not with your heel. That way, your foot can pass on the force well and your ankle can act as a spring. Smooth, round pedalling protects your knees and saves energy. With the right gear, you can keep a comfortable pedalling speed even when it gets steep.

There are simple flat pedals, pedals with pins for mountain bikes and **clipless pedals**, where the shoe clicks in with a cleat. With these you can pull as well as push. In Switzerland, the law requires orange or yellow **reflectors** on the pedals. They move up and down as you ride and so are especially noticeable to drivers at night.

Karl Drais's first running machine from 1817 had no pedals at all; you pushed yourself along the ground with your feet. In the 1860s in France, cranks with pedals were fitted directly to the front wheel. Because each turn only took you one wheel's circumference forward, penny-farthings with huge front wheels were later built. Only with the chain, from about 1885, did the bicycle as we know it today come about.

begriffe.erklaerung: The arm the pedal is attached to, which turns in a circle.
A rod with which you can increase a force.
How strongly a force makes something turn.
A part that reflects light so that you can be seen in the dark.

gewusst: The left pedal has a left-hand thread so that it does not come loose by itself while riding.
The name pedelec for e-bikes comes from the English “pedal electric cycle”.
The word pedal comes from the Latin word for foot, “pes”.

teile.einleitung: Pascal's principle says that pressure in an enclosed liquid spreads out equally everywhere. With this simple law, you can lift a whole car with a small force. It is found in car brakes, vehicle lifts, excavators and hydraulic presses.
wichtigste: Pressure in an enclosed liquid spreads equally in all directions.
The principle is named after the 17th-century French scholar Blaise Pascal.
Pressure is calculated as force divided by area.
In a hydraulic press, a small piston produces a much larger force on the large piston.
What you gain in force, you pay for in distance; the work stays the same.
Hydraulic brakes in cars are based on Pascal's principle.
Liquids such as oil are used because they can hardly be compressed.

abschnitte.text: If you press on a liquid in a closed container, the **pressure** rises by the same amount everywhere in the liquid. It acts in all directions and equally strongly at every point on the wall. You can try this with a water bag with several small holes: if you squeeze the bag, water squirts out of all the holes at the same time. Blaise Pascal described this law in the 17th century.

A **hydraulic press** consists of two connected cylinders with pistons of different sizes. If you press with 50 newtons on a small piston with an area of 2 square centimetres, a certain pressure is produced. This pressure also acts on the large piston of 200 square centimetres, which is a hundred times larger. That is why the large piston pushes upwards with 5000 newtons, a hundred times as hard.

This increase in force is not completely free. The small piston has to travel a much longer **distance** than the large one, a hundred times longer in the example. The **work**, that is force times distance, is the same at both pistons if friction is ignored. It is like a lever or a pulley: you save force but need more distance.

When you press the brake pedal in a car, a piston in the **master cylinder** presses on the brake fluid. The pressure, for example 40 bar, acts equally strongly in every wheel cylinder through thin pipes and presses the brake pads on. In garages, **vehicle lifts** raise cars with a weight of 12,000 newtons, and only 200 newtons are needed at the small piston if the areas are 0.0005 and 0.03 square metres. Excavators, cranes, snow groomers and office chairs also work with hydraulics.

Hydraulics needs a liquid that can hardly be **compressed**, usually a special oil. Air, on the other hand, is springy and can be squeezed together, so part of the force would be lost. That is why air in a brake pipe is dangerous: the brake pedal then feels spongy. For calculations: 300 newtons on 15 square centimetres give 200,000 pascals, that is 2 bar.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on an area, measured in pascals or bar.
A movable plug that slides back and forth in a cylinder.
Technology that transmits forces with the help of liquids.
A special liquid that carries the pressure from the pedal to the wheels in a car.

gewusst: In a famous experiment, Pascal is said to have burst a barrel with a long, thin pipe full of water.
A snow groomer in Swiss ski resorts moves its large blade with hydraulics.
Spiders also stretch their legs with fluid pressure instead of muscles.

teile.einleitung: The Pauli principle is a basic rule of quantum physics: two electrons in an atom may never be in exactly the same state. The physicist Wolfgang Pauli formulated it in 1925. Without this principle there would be no periodic table, no chemistry and no solid objects as we know them.
wichtigste: The Pauli principle is also called the exclusion principle.
It applies to fermions, particles with half-integer spin such as electrons, protons and neutrons.
Wolfgang Pauli formulated it in 1925 and received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1945.
An orbital can hold at most 2 electrons, and their spins are opposite.
The shell with n = 3 holds at most 18 electrons.
Electron degeneracy pressure stops white dwarfs from collapsing.
Pauli taught at ETH Zurich from 1928.

abschnitte.text: Every electron in an atom is described by four **quantum numbers**, a kind of address. The Pauli principle says that two electrons in the same atom may never match in all four quantum numbers. At least one must be different. You can picture it like a cinema, where only one person may sit in each seat.

Electrons have a property called **spin**, which, put simply, you can imagine as a tiny rotation. Spin can only have two values, “up” or “down”. That is why an **orbital**, a region where the electrons are found, can hold at most two electrons with opposite spins. In the ground state of a helium atom, the two electrons sit in the same orbital and have antiparallel spins.

Because the electrons cannot all fit into the lowest state, they spread out over **shells**. A shell with principal quantum number n holds at most 2 times n times n electrons: 2 in the first, 8 in the second, 18 in the third shell. This gives the structure of the **periodic table** of the elements. So the Pauli principle explains why sodium reacts quite differently from neon.

Because of the Pauli principle, electrons that are squeezed tightly together resist being squeezed any further. This **degeneracy pressure** keeps white dwarfs, the remains of Sun-like stars, stable. In metals, the electrons fill the states from the bottom up. The energy of the highest occupied state at absolute zero is called the **Fermi energy**.

Wolfgang Pauli was born in Vienna in 1900 and was already a child prodigy of physics as a student. From 1928 he was a professor at **ETH Zurich** and lived in Zurich until his death in 1958. He was known for his sharp criticism of unclear ideas. Physicists jokingly talked about the “Pauli effect”: experiments and equipment were said to fail often when he was nearby.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle with half-integer spin, for example an electron.
A quantum property of a particle; put simply, a kind of self-rotation.
A region around the atomic nucleus where electrons are found.
A number that describes a particular state of a particle.
A small, very dense remnant of a burnt-out star.

gewusst: The fact that you do not fall through the floor is closely linked to the Pauli principle.
A teaspoon of material from a white dwarf would weigh several tonnes on Earth.
Pauli predicted that there must be a tiny, barely detectable particle, which was later called the neutrino.

teile.einleitung: The Paul Scherrer Institute, PSI for short, is the largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering in Switzerland. It lies on the River Aare in the canton of Aargau and runs huge research facilities that exist nowhere else in Switzerland. Researchers from all over the world come here to look into tiny structures with particle beams and especially bright light.
wichtigste: PSI is located mainly in the Aargau municipality of Villigen.
It belongs to the ETH Domain, like ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne.
It is named after Paul Scherrer, a physicist at ETH Zurich.
PSI was created in 1988 from two predecessor institutes, EIR and SIN.
The Swiss Light Source is a synchrotron light source that produces extremely bright X-ray light.
SwissFEL produces very short and intense X-ray laser pulses.
Cancer patients are treated with proton therapy at PSI.

abschnitte.text: PSI lies on both sides of the **River Aare**, in the municipalities of Villigen and Würenlingen. It was founded in 1988 by merging the Federal Institute for Reactor Research (**EIR**) and the Swiss Institute for Nuclear Research (**SIN**). Today more than 2000 people work there. The institute belongs to the ETH Domain and is funded mainly by the federal government.

**Paul Scherrer** lived from 1890 to 1969 and was a professor of physics at ETH Zurich. Among other things, he studied crystals with X-rays and built up nuclear physics in Switzerland. He was considered an inspiring teacher and encouraged many young researchers. In his honour, the new institute was given his name in 1988.

The **Swiss Light Source** is a ring-shaped particle accelerator in which electrons circle at almost the speed of light. As they do, they give off extremely bright X-ray light, which is used, for example, to study the structure of proteins or new materials. **SwissFEL** is an X-ray laser that has been in operation since 2016. Its flashes of light are so short that they can be used to watch chemical reactions almost in slow motion.

The heart of the proton facility is a large **ring cyclotron**, which brings protons to very high speeds. These protons are used to produce other particles. The SINQ neutron source supplies neutrons that let you look inside materials. The SμS source supplies **muons**, short-lived elementary particles used to study the magnetic properties of materials.

PSI has a centre for **proton therapy**. In it, tumours are treated very precisely with a beam of protons. The advantage is that the healthy tissue around the tumour is better protected. This is especially important for children and for tumours close to sensitive organs such as the eyes or the brain.

PSI does not only research the basics but also practical questions. These include batteries, fuel cells, renewable energy and the safety of nuclear power stations. Air pollutants and the climate are also studied. In the school laboratory **iLab**, school classes can do physics experiments themselves.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ring-shaped particle accelerator in which particles fly in a circle and give off light.
An accelerator in which particles get faster and faster on a spiral path.
Cancer treatment with a beam of protons instead of X-rays.
An elementary particle similar to the electron but much heavier, which decays quickly.
The group made up of the two federal institutes of technology and four federal research institutes.

gewusst: SwissFEL is housed in a building around 740 metres long in the forest.
At PSI, the masses and properties of particles have been measured that appear in textbooks all over the world.
Every year, several thousand guest researchers from abroad come to PSI.

teile.einleitung: A parabolic flight is a special flight manoeuvre in which people on board an aircraft float weightless for a short time. To do this, the aircraft flies a path in the shape of an arch, a parabola. Researchers and astronauts use these flights to carry out experiments and to train for space.
wichtigste: On a parabolic flight, an aircraft flies an arch-shaped path, a parabola.
One parabola gives about 22 seconds of weightlessness.
Before and after the weightless phase, you are pressed into your seat with about 1.8 times normal gravity.
A European research flight typically includes about 30 parabolas.
In Europe, the Airbus A310 Zero G is used for this (as of 2026).
The lower gravity on the Moon or Mars can also be recreated.
Many people on board feel sick because their sense of balance gets confused.

abschnitte.text: On a parabolic flight, a large aircraft takes turns flying steeply upwards and back down again. At the top of the arch, the aircraft and the people inside are all in **free fall** together. Because everything falls at the same speed, the people float in the cabin. This state is called **weightlessness**, even though the Earth of course keeps pulling.

First the aircraft flies level and then pulls steeply upwards, pressing the people into their seats with about 1.8 times normal gravity. Then the pilot reduces the thrust so far that the aircraft flies a **ballistic parabola**, like a thrown ball. The engines keep running, but only to make up for air resistance. After about 22 seconds of floating, the pilot pulls the aircraft out again, and once more about 1.8 times normal gravity acts.

Parabolic flights are used mainly for **experiments** and for astronaut training. Researchers study, for example, how flames, liquids or plants react without gravity. Astronauts practise moving and working while floating. If the aircraft flies flatter arches, gravity is only reduced, so the conditions on the **Moon** or Mars can be recreated.

In Europe, the French company **Novespace** organises the flights, usually from Bordeaux, on behalf of space agencies such as ESA. It uses the converted Airbus A310 Zero G, which used to serve as a government aircraft. In the cabin, most of the seats have been removed and the walls and floor are padded. Swiss research groups, for example from the University of Zurich, have also carried out experiments on parabolic flights.

abschnitte.titel: The body on a roller coaster
abschnitte.text: The constant switching between heavy and weightless confuses the **organ of balance** in the inner ear. The eyes and the ear tell the brain contradictory things, and many people feel sick. That is why participants are often given a medicine against travel sickness beforehand. Because of this effect, NASA's aircraft got the nickname “Vomit Comet”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state in which you feel nothing of your weight and float.
An arch-shaped curve, like the path of a thrown ball.
Movement in which only gravity acts on an object.
The part of the inner ear that senses how we move and which way is up.

gewusst: A flight with about 30 parabolas adds up to around ten minutes of weightlessness altogether.
Film scenes set in space have been shot in parabolic flight aircraft so that the actors really float.
The International Space Station is constantly in free fall around the Earth, like an endless parabolic flight.

teile.einleitung: A paper bridge is a simple experiment that lets you learn in a playful way how bridges and building parts become stable. A flat sheet of paper carries almost nothing, but a folded sheet carries a surprising amount. The secret is not in the material but in the shape.
wichtigste: A flat sheet between two cups bends under a single coin.
If you fold the paper in a zigzag, the bridge carries much more.
The folds make the paper stiffer, because it can no longer bend so easily.
A sheet rolled into a tube and stood upright carries a surprising amount.
To test it, it is best to put coins on the bridge as weights.
Corrugated cardboard, corrugated iron and steel girders use the same principle.
Engineers call building with clever shapes lightweight construction.

abschnitte.text: You place two cups or piles of books of the same height about 15 centimetres apart. You lay a flat sheet of paper across them as a **bridge**. Even a single coin in the middle makes the sheet sag and fall down. Then you fold a sheet of the same size in a **zigzag** like an accordion and lay it across the gap again. Now you can stack coin after coin on it, often many dozens.

A flat sheet is very thin, so it bends easily. With the folds, the paper sticks out above and below the middle. If the folded bridge wants to bend, the top side has to be squashed and the bottom side stretched, and that takes much more force. This makes the paper **stiffer**, even though it is still the same sheet. Experts say that the shape increases the **bending stiffness**.

If you roll a sheet into a **tube** and stand it upright, it becomes a column. You can put surprisingly heavy things on it, sometimes even a book. The weight is spread evenly over the whole round wall. Only when the wall buckles somewhere does the column collapse. Several tubes side by side carry even more.

**Corrugated cardboard** consists of two flat layers of paper with a wavy layer in between, which is why cardboard boxes are so stable. The roofs of barns and halls are often made of corrugated iron. Steel girders on building sites are shaped like an I or H so that they carry a lot with little material. Bridges, too, often have frameworks of triangles or hollow boxes instead of thick, solid beams. Nature uses the principle as well, for example in hollow blades of grass and birds' bones.

Paper bridges are a popular experiment in lessons and competitions. Often the rule is to build the strongest possible bridge with just one sheet and no glue. You can test different shapes: zigzags, tubes, arches or U-shapes. It is worth counting the coins carefully and noting the results in a table. That way you work like real **researchers**.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly something resists bending or changing shape.
Cardboard with a wavy paper layer in the middle, which is light yet stable.
An upright building part that carries weight from above.
Building with as little material as possible but with clever, stable shapes.

gewusst: A sheet folded in a zigzag can carry many times its own weight.
Hollow tubes are almost as stable as solid rods but much lighter.
Blades of grass are hollow and bend in the wind without breaking.

teile.einleitung: A periscope, called a Sehrohr (seeing tube) in German, is an optical device that lets you look over obstacles without being seen yourself. It is best known from submarines, which use it to look above the surface of the water. You can make a simple periscope yourself with two mirrors and some cardboard.
wichtigste: In German, a periscope is called a Sehrohr.
The word comes from Greek and means roughly “look around”.
A simple periscope needs 2 mirrors.
The two mirrors are tilted at an angle and parallel to each other.
The image in a simple periscope with two mirrors is upright.
Submarines use periscopes to look over the water.
On land you can use one, for example, to look over a wall.

abschnitte.text: A periscope is a tube that sends light round two corners. At the top, an opening looks in one direction; at the bottom, you look in facing the same direction. This lets you see what is happening above or behind an **obstacle**. The name comes from the Greek words “peri” for around and “skopein” for look.

In the simplest periscope there is a **mirror** at the top and one at the bottom, both tilted at an angle of 45 degrees. Light falls on the first mirror at the top and is sent downwards. The second mirror sends it horizontally into the eye again. Here the **law of reflection** applies: light is reflected at the same angle at which it hits the mirror. Because there are two reflections, the image ends up upright and not reversed left to right.

A **submarine** can stay just below the surface of the water and poke out only the slim periscope. This lets the crew see ships and coasts while staying almost invisible themselves. Such periscopes are several metres long and contain prisms and lenses instead of simple mirrors, so that you can zoom in. Modern submarines also use cameras that send the image to screens.

In the First World War, soldiers used periscopes to look out of the trenches without raising their heads. Tanks also have angled mirrors with which the crew can look out while staying protected. In large crowds, for example at parades, spectators sometimes hold small **cardboard periscopes** above other people's heads. In medicine and engineering, there are similar devices for looking into narrow spaces.

You can build a simple periscope from a long **cardboard tube**, for example a milk carton, and two small mirrors. You cut a window at the top and one at the bottom on opposite sides. You stick the mirrors in at an angle of 45 degrees so that they are parallel to each other. Now you can look over the edge of the table or round a corner.

begriffe.erklaerung: A smooth surface that reflects light.
The bouncing back of light from a surface.
A transparent, cut piece of glass that can redirect light.
A ship that can travel under water.

gewusst: By turning the periscope in a submarine, you can search the whole horizon all the way round.
A single mirror shows the world reversed left to right, but a periscope with two mirrors shows it the right way round.
When a submarine travels with its periscope up, it makes a small wave by which the periscope can be spotted from far away.

teile.einleitung: A pendulum is an object that hangs from a thread or rod and swings back and forth. Swings, pendulum clocks and wrecking balls are examples. With a pendulum, you can see wonderfully how energy changes from one form into another.
wichtigste: A pendulum swings back and forth around its lowest position.
At the lowest point it is fastest and has the most kinetic energy.
At the turning points the speed is zero, and the energy is all potential energy.
For small swings, the period depends mainly on the length.
A pendulum about 1 m long takes about 2 seconds for a whole swing.
Christiaan Huygens invented the pendulum clock in 1656.
In 1851 in Paris, Léon Foucault used a pendulum to show the rotation of the Earth.

abschnitte.text: A **pendulum** is an object that can swing on a thread, rope or rod around a point it hangs from. If you pull it to the side and let go, gravity pulls it back down. Because it has momentum, it swings past the lowest point to the other side. The outermost points, where it stands still for a moment, are called **turning points**.

At the turning points, the pendulum is at its highest and stands still for a moment; its energy is all **potential energy**. As it swings down, the potential energy turns into **kinetic energy**, and at the lowest point it is fastest. Then it rises again, and the kinetic energy turns back into potential energy. If a pendulum is raised 20 cm, it travels at about 1.98 m/s at the bottom, without friction.

For small swings, the time of one swing depends almost only on the **length** of the pendulum. How heavy the bob is, on the other hand, makes no difference. A pendulum about 1 m long takes about 2 seconds to go there and back once. A pendulum four times as long swings only half as fast, so it takes twice as long.

According to legend, around 1583 Galileo Galilei watched a swinging lamp in Pisa Cathedral and noticed that every swing took the same time. The Dutchman **Christiaan Huygens** invented the pendulum clock in 1656, which was much more accurate than earlier clocks. In 1851, **Léon Foucault** set a long pendulum swinging in Paris whose plane of swing seemed to turn slowly. This proved that in reality the Earth is turning beneath the pendulum.

A swing is a pendulum too. To keep it from stopping, you have to add energy in the right rhythm, for example by swinging your legs. A real pendulum always gets slower, because air resistance and **friction** turn energy into heat. Without a drive, it eventually comes to rest.

In old grandfather clocks and cuckoo clocks, the pendulum sets the rhythm. A metronome helps musicians play evenly. On building sites, houses used to be knocked down with a heavy **wrecking ball** that swings like a pendulum. Some very tall skyscrapers have huge pendulums hanging inside that damp the swaying in the wind.

begriffe.erklaerung: The outermost point where the pendulum stands still for a moment and turns back.
The time for one whole swing, there and back.
Energy an object has because it is high up.
Energy an object has because it is moving.

gewusst: A pendulum whose half swing lasts exactly one second is called a seconds pendulum; it is just under a metre long.
Pendulum clocks were the most accurate clocks in the world for around 250 years.
On the Moon, the same pendulum would swing much more slowly than on Earth, because gravity is weaker there.

teile.einleitung: The period is the time an oscillation takes for one complete cycle. For a pendulum, it is the time to go there and back once. It can be used to build clocks, describe sounds and compare many processes in nature.
wichtigste: The period is the time for one complete back-and-forth movement.
It is given the letter T and is measured in seconds.
Frequency is the reciprocal: frequency equals 1 divided by the period.
A tuning fork at 440 hertz has a period of about 2.3 milliseconds.
In experiments, you usually time ten oscillations and divide by ten so that reaction time matters less.
The period of a pendulum depends mainly on its length.
Going from one turning point to the other takes only half a period.

abschnitte.text: Many movements repeat themselves again and again, for example a pendulum, a swing or a guitar string. Such a movement is called an **oscillation**. The time for one complete cycle, until everything is exactly the same again, is called the **period** T. If a swing goes from right at the front to right at the back in 0.8 seconds, the period is 1.6 seconds, because it also has to come back again.

The **frequency** tells you how many oscillations happen per second, measured in hertz. It is the reciprocal of the period. If a pendulum makes exactly 20 swings in 36 seconds, one swing lasts 1.8 seconds and the frequency is about 0.56 hertz. For the note A of a tuning fork at 440 hertz, one oscillation lasts only about 2.3 milliseconds.

Timing a single swing with a stopwatch is inaccurate, because we press about a tenth of a second too late. This **reaction time** matters less if you time ten swings and divide the result by ten. It is best to start timing when the pendulum passes through its lowest point. Swinging in step is interesting too: two pendulums with periods of 2.0 and 2.1 seconds are at the same point at the same time again after 42 seconds.

For a **simple pendulum**, the period depends almost only on the length and hardly on the mass or how far it swings. Galileo Galilei is said to have noticed this from a swinging chandelier in Pisa Cathedral. The Dutchman Christiaan Huygens built the first **pendulum clock** in 1656. A pendulum just under a metre long has a period of about 2 seconds, so it swings from one side to the other once a second.

In heat, a metal pendulum rod expands a little, the pendulum gets longer and swings more slowly. The clock then loses time. If a pendulum clock gains time, you move the **pendulum bob** down a little so that the pendulum gets longer. Clockmakers used to build special pendulums from different metals that balanced each other out.

begriffe.erklaerung: A movement that repeats itself regularly.
The number of oscillations per second, measured in hertz.
The unit of frequency; 1 hertz is one oscillation per second.
The point where a pendulum stands still for a moment and turns back.
The time we need to react to something.

gewusst: The Earth has periods too: it turns on its own axis in about a day and goes round the Sun in about a year.
A pendulum on the Moon would swing much more slowly than on Earth.
The quartz crystals in wristwatches usually oscillate more than 32,000 times a second.

teile.einleitung: The pascal is the unit of pressure, abbreviated Pa. One pascal is a very small pressure, roughly as much as a sheet of paper lying flat on a table exerts. That is why larger units such as hectopascals are often used in everyday life, for the weather.
wichtigste: One pascal equals 1 newton per square metre.
The unit is named after the French scholar Blaise Pascal.
Blaise Pascal lived in the 17th century and built a mechanical calculating machine when he was still a young man.
1 hectopascal is 100 Pa, 1 kilopascal 1000 Pa and 1 megapascal 1,000,000 Pa.
At sea level, the average air pressure is about 1013 hectopascals.
One pascal is roughly the pressure of a sheet of paper lying flat.
The pascal is the official unit of pressure in the International System of Units, SI.

abschnitte.text: **Pressure** tells you how strongly a force presses on an area. It is calculated as force divided by area. If a force of 1 newton presses evenly on an area of 1 square metre, the pressure is 1 **pascal**. That is very little, because 1 newton is roughly the weight of a small 100-gram bar of chocolate.

Because a pascal is so small, prefixes are usually needed. 1 **hectopascal** (hPa) is 100 Pa, 1 kilopascal (kPa) is 1000 Pa and 1 megapascal (MPa) is a million Pa. The **bar** is also very common: 1 bar equals 100,000 Pa. Bicycle and car tyres are usually pumped up to a few bar.

Weather reports give the **air pressure** in hectopascals. At sea level it averages about 1013 hPa. Higher up it is lower; at the Jungfraujoch, at around 3500 metres, it is only about two thirds of that. High air pressure often brings fine weather, low air pressure more likely clouds and rain.

Blaise Pascal was born in France in 1623 and died in 1662. At about 19 he built a **calculating machine** to help his father with tax calculations; it is called the Pascaline. He researched air pressure and in 1648 had measurements taken on the Puy de Dôme mountain showing that air pressure decreases with height. He was also an important mathematician and thinker.

In everyday life, we come across pressures from tiny to enormous. A sheet of paper lying flat presses on the table with about 1 Pa. The air pressure around us is about 100,000 Pa; we just do not feel it, because it presses equally from all sides. In engineering, the strength of steel or concrete is measured in **megapascals**, and at the deepest point of the ocean there is a pressure of over 100 megapascals.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on a certain area.
The unit of force.
100 pascals, the unit for air pressure in the weather report.
A unit of pressure; 1 bar is 100,000 pascals.
The International System of Units, which applies to measurements worldwide.

gewusst: The programming language Pascal is also named after Blaise Pascal.
Air pressure used to be given in millibars in the weather report; one millibar is exactly one hectopascal.
The pressure under a pointed stiletto heel can be greater than under an elephant's foot.
